raw_case_text:
A 43-year-old man was admitted to our neurological department reporting lumbar arthralgia, right leg pain, and mild muscle weakness. Upon neurological examination, he exhibited paralysis of the left arm and forearm, limited finger mobility, weakness in the right lower limb, and deviation of the oral rim to the left. A swallowing assessment revealed mild oropharyngeal muscles paralysis. No speech disorder was detected.
His medical history included a diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis, confirmed by positive Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA)-B27. In the six months prior to hospitalization, he had undergone intravenous antibiotic therapy (imipenem and linezolid) for suspected cerebral nocardiosis, with subsequent clinical and radiological improvement. Additionally, he had a biopsy of a palmar lesion, which indicated lobular and septal panniculitis.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed two contrast-enhancing lesions at the cortical-subcortical junction: one in the right posterior temporal region and another in the left anterior frontal region. During his hospital stay, he experienced generalized tonic-clonic seizures and flaccid paralysis of the lower limbs, accompanied by fever spikes. A subsequent brain and spine MRI showed a new hyperintense lesion in the left middle frontal gyrus on FLAIR sequences (Figure 1(a)), as well as pathological enhancement along the right ventral pontine rim (Figure 1(b)) and towards the right Meckel's cave (Figure 1(c)). Furthermore, there was suspicion of myelitis affecting the spinal cord from T3 to T12 (Figure 1(d)).
Despite extensive blood and cerebrospinal fluid tests, no significant abnormalities were found, ruling out systemic spread of infectious disease. After multidisciplinary consultation, a decision was made to perform a cerebral biopsy targeting the largest, most accessible lesion in the left frontal region. Despite being informed of the risks, the patient consented to the procedure.
Upon awakening from the biopsy, the patient exhibited trismus (clenched jaw) and paralysis of facial muscles with an inability to voluntarily open his mouth or move his tongue and a consequent anarthria. Classical causes such as drug side effects, tetanus, or infections were ruled out, as blood tests, cultures, and a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis were repeated, all of which were within normal limits. Acute lesions in the contralateral opercular area were ruled out through radiological imaging; both head CT and MRI showed the presence of the surgical cavity (yellow arrows), without any ischemic or hemorrhagic lesions (Figures 2 and 3). The patient was still able to sleep with his mouth open and with involuntary facial movements present. A swallowing assessment showed paralysis of pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles, so a nasogastric tube was inserted for medication and feeding, and oral carbamazepine and baclofen were initiated in order to modulate muscle tone. Over 3 months, there was gradual improvement in trismus, although anarthria persisted. Histological analysis of the biopsy revealed nonspecific inflammatory tissue.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old man presented with lumbar arthralgia, right leg pain, and mild muscle weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was admitted to the neurology department with lumbar arthralgia, right leg pain, and mild muscle weakness. Six months prior, he had been treated with intravenous imipenem and linezolid for suspected cerebral nocardiosis with clinical and radiological improvement. During hospitalization, he developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures, flaccid paraplegia, and fever spikes.
subjective.past_medical_history: HLA-B27-positive ankylosing spondylitis; suspected cerebral nocardiosis 6 months prior treated with IV imipenem and linezolid; prior palmar lesion biopsy showing lobular and septal panniculitis.

objective.physical_examination: Initial neurological examination revealed left arm and forearm paralysis, limited finger mobility, right lower limb weakness, leftward deviation of the oral rim, and mild oropharyngeal muscle paralysis on swallowing assessment without speech disorder. Immediately following left frontal brain biopsy, he developed acute trismus (clenched jaw), bilateral voluntary facial/lingual paralysis, pharyngeal/laryngeal paralysis, and complete anarthria with preserved involuntary laughing/yawning and mouth opening during sleep (Foix-Chavany-Marie syndrome).
objective.routine_investigations: Extensive blood tests and cultures were within normal limits and negative for systemic infection or tetanus.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission brain MRI showed two contrast-enhancing cortical-subcortical lesions in the right posterior temporal and left anterior frontal regions. Repeat brain and spine MRI after inpatient seizures and paraplegia revealed a new FLAIR-hyperintense lesion in the left middle frontal gyrus, pathological enhancement along the right ventral pontine rim extending toward the right Meckel's cave, and suspected thoracic myelitis from T3 to T12. Repeated lumbar punctures and CSF analyses were normal. Post-biopsy head CT and MRI showed only the left frontal surgical cavity without contralateral opercular ischemia or hemorrhage. Histopathology of the left frontal brain biopsy revealed nonspecific inflammatory tissue.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Multifocal central nervous system inflammatory lesions (nonspecific inflammatory tissue on left frontal brain biopsy, with active infection and tetanus ruled out on blood and CSF analyses) complicated post-operatively by bilateral anterior opercular syndrome (Foix-Chavany-Marie syndrome) with trismus and anarthria. Management included nasogastric tube placement for nutrition and medication delivery, alongside oral carbamazepine and baclofen to modulate muscle tone. Over 3 months of follow-up, trismus gradually improved while anarthria persisted.
